title: Councils continue
hookLine: since Vatican II, bishops meet in synods, including recent ones where laypeople also voted

cards: Round tables in a big hall in Rome. At each one, a handful of people: a cardinal, a parish priest, a sister, a young mother, a theology professor.

They take turns speaking, and the rule is that each person finishes before anyone answers. Then there's silence, and prayer, and another round. It looks less like a parliament than a long family dinner.
This is what a gathering of the Church can look like now, and it has an old Greek name: synod.

teach.b: Synod is a Greek word for a meeting or assembly of the Church. Pope Francis has explained it simply: walking together. Here's how the habit grew.
Bishops at Vatican Two wanted bishops from around the world to help the pope in caring for the whole Church.

While the council was still meeting, Pope Paul the Sixth set up the Synod of Bishops, a gathering that meets again and again in Rome, between councils, on questions like the family, young people, or the Word of God.
In recent synods, laypeople, women and men, sat at the tables, and some of them voted alongside the bishops.
Before the meetings, parishes around the world were asked to listen to their own people and send up what they heard. Third, the method.
Pope Francis has described a synodal Church as one that listens, where each person has something to learn from the others.
Catholics differ about how far this should go and what it should decide; that argument is itself part of the walk. Fourth, the oldest picture.

On the road to Emmaus, two disciples were walking and reasoning together, and in the Douay-Rheims, "Jesus himself also drawing near, went with them." He listened first, and asked them what they were talking about.
Over the last thirty days this path has walked from Nicaea through Ephesus and Chalcedon, to Trent and both Vatican councils. The meetings never really stopped.

how: The Synod of Bishops meets in Rome on topics the pope chooses, and before recent synods dioceses and parishes held listening sessions; some laypeople have also taken part and voted.

games.q: you're at a synod table. someone says something you strongly disagree with. by the synod's method, what's next?
o: let them finish, keep silence, then speak in your turn.
games.why: the synodal method asks each person to finish, with silence and prayer before the next round, so that everyone listens first.

practice: Recall the last conversation where you were already composing your answer while the other person talked, and replay it slowly, this time hearing them out to the end of every sentence.
Saint James put it this way: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak." If you pray, ask for that patience.

wordCard.voice: Synod. A gathering of the Church, which Pope Francis calls walking together; since the council, bishops and now laypeople meet in synods. Today's word.
